extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, translators, and educated readers interested in style and composition
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance drawn from Coleridge's literary notes and footnotes on poetry, prose, translation, parody, and the habits of readers/writers. Emphasizes principles of imagery, diction, reasoned argument, and craft for writers and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of imagery / avoid absurd exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: “the likeness is lost, while the likeness in the effects is rendered absurd by the exaggeration. In Spenser and Fletcher the thought is justifiable; for the images are at least consistent...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep images and allegory internally consistent. Exaggeration that breaks the internal likeness or mixes incompatible images renders effects absurd rather than effective. Ensure any allegorical device or 'visualized pun' coheres across instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dependence on personal malignity or gratuitous naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Especially in this age of personality... when the meanest insects are worshipped... if only the brainless head be atoned for by the sting of personal malignity in the tail;--when the most vapid satires have become the objects of a keen public interest, purely from the number of contemporary characters named...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make a work's interest rest on naming contemporary persons or on malicious gossip. Satire that relies chiefly on personal invective or 'patch-work notes' naming characters weakens literary merit and confuses lasting value with ephemeral curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not tell only half the fact (avoid deceptive partiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: This is one instance among many of deception, by the telling the half of a fact, and omitting the other half, when it is from their mutual counteraction and neutralization, that the whole truth arises...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting partial truths that distort meaning by omission. In criticism and narrative, consider interacting or neutralizing components: the whole truth may arise only from the balance of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize complex faculties without isolating components
rubrics_metrics.description: Great wit (meaning genius) to madness sure is near allied. Now if the profound sensibility... were alone considered... it might be fairly described as exposing the individual to a greater chance of mental derangement; but then a more than usual rapidity of association... is a component equally essential; and to the due modification of each by the other the genius itself consists...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing capacities like 'genius', avoid reducing them to a single trait. Recognize multiple interacting components (e.g., sensibility and rapid association) and show how they modify one another; beware of simplistic aphorisms that conflate or isolate causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish active reading from passive pastime
rubrics_metrics.description: For as to the devotees of the circulating libraries, I dare not compliment their pass-time, or rather kill-time, with the name of reading. Call it rather a sort of beggarly day-dreaming... the mind of the dreamer furnishes for itself nothing but laziness, and a little mawkish sensibility; while the whole materiel and imagery of the doze is supplied ab extra by a sort of mental camera obscura manufactured at the printing office...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value reading that engages, questions, and produces thought. Avoid catering to or producing writing that simply supplies mental images for passive consumption. Writers should aim to stimulate reflection rather than merely soothe or occupy idle attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compilation, selection and arrangement should preserve imaginative and reflective power
rubrics_metrics.description: none, which uniting the charms of romance and history, keeps the imagination so constantly on the wing, and yet leaves so much for after reflection... a compilation, which, in the various excellencies of translation, selection, and arrangement, required and proves greater genius in the compiler...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In edited or compiled works (translations, anthologies), selection and arrangement are creative acts: preserve imaginative momentum while leaving space for reader reflection. Good compilation can require as much genius as original composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid juxtaposing incompatible thoughts without showing linkage (avoid 'bulls')
rubrics_metrics.description: The bull namely consists in the bringing her two incompatible thoughts, with the sensation, but without the sense, of their connection... The man feels as if he were standing on his head though he cannot but see that he is truly standing on his feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not place irreconcilable ideas side-by-side without demonstrating the transitional or mediating concepts. Clarity requires signaling how apparently contrary notions relate; otherwise the reader experiences incoherence rather than insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and imitation must balance likeness with difference
rubrics_metrics.description: to conceal and convey wit and wisdom in the semblance of folly and dulness... is doubtless a proof of genius... but that the attempt to ridicule a silly and childish poem, by writing another still sillier and still more childish, can only prove... that the parodist is a still greater blockhead than the original writer... The difference which must blend with and balance the likeness, in order to constitute a just imitation...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful parody or mimicry requires artful contrast: preserve recognizable likeness while adding distinctive, illuminating difference. Mere escalation of defects produces a worse copy and no satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid harsh and obscure construction in verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Wordsworth... is more free from this latter defect than most of the young poets his contemporaries. It may however be exemplified, together with the harsh and obscure construction, in which he more often offended, in the following lines:... (example lines)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clarity and smooth construction in poetic diction. Harsh, obscure syntax obstructs meaning and weakens the poem; revise early poems that display such defects before republication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in vocabulary: distinguish meanings to avoid equivocation
rubrics_metrics.description: This is effected either by giving to the one word a general, and to the other an exclusive use; as “to put on the back” and 'to indorse;' or by an actual distinction of meanings... When two distinct meanings are confounded under one or more words... erroneous consequences will be drawn...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be disciplined about word choice: where words have multiple senses, assign clear uses or coin/appropriate terms to prevent equivocation. Distinguishing nuances prevents false inferences and clarifies argument and imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that 'common sense' and technical terms shift historically
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense, therefore, differs in different ages. What was born and christened in the Schools passes by degrees into the world at large, and becomes the property of the market and the tea-table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing terms like 'common sense' or inherited technical words, be aware of their historical shifts in meaning. Writers and critics should indicate sense or define terms where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define technical philosophical words carefully (example: 'idea')
rubrics_metrics.description: I here use the word idea in Mr. Hume’s sense on account of its general currency amongst the English metaphysicians; though against my own judgment, for I believe that the vague use of this word has been the cause of much error and more confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inoretical or philosophical writing, explicitly state intended meaning of contested terms to avoid confusion and error. Prefer precise definitions over casual usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neologisms are permissible when they preserve logical or rhetorical harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: I have therefore hazarded the word, intensify: though, I confess, it sounds uncouth to my own ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coin or adopt new terms when necessary to avoid ambiguity and to sustain sentence harmony, but be mindful of potential awkwardness; justify neologisms by their utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited vocabulary can foster rich metaphorical language but beware overreliance
rubrics_metrics.description: An American Indian with little variety of images, and a still scantier stock of language, is obliged to turn his few words to many purposes, by likenesses so clear and analogies so remote as to give his language the semblance and character of lyric poetry interspersed with grotesques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A constrained lexicon can encourage striking analogies and concentrated imagery; however, avoid overusing a single source or rhetorical reservoir (e.g., over-reliance on biblical images) to the point of sterility or caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical and scholarly writing: favor strong reasoning and copious induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The merit... consists in the masterly force of reasoning, and the copiousness of induction, with which he has assailed, and (in my opinion) subverted the tyranny of the mechanic system in physiology...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support claims with rigorous argumentation and abundant empirical or textual examples. Originality combined with thorough induction secures lasting scholarly value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid category-errors in argument (apply forms of reasoning appropriately)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever A=B, and A is not=B, are equally demonstrable... the faculty and forms of reasoning employed are inapplicable to the subject--i.e. that there is a metabasis eis allo genos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that logical forms and attributes are applied only to compatible categories. If reasoning yields contradictions, reassess whether the method or concepts are appropriate to the subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn a language by naming objects and imitating native speech
rubrics_metrics.description: it may be useful... the incalculable advantage which I derived from learning all the words, that could possibly be so learned, with the objects before me... to call every, the minutest, thing by its German name... ask the mother in the house, the children in the lanes... and look at the moves of their mouths while they are talking...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For translation and language acquisition, learn vocabulary in situ with real objects and imitate native speakers (including colloquial and idiomatic speech). Prioritize spoken usage and living idiom over bookish equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine elevated feeling with natural images for strongest poetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Most interesting is it to consider the effect, when the feelings are wrought above the natural pitch by the belief of something mysterious, while all the images are purely natural. Then it is, that religion and poetry strike deepest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maximize emotional and aesthetic impact, pair intense or elevated sentiments (often involving belief or mystery) with concrete, natural imagery rather than loftily abstract or artificial pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature or excessive authorship; allow thoughts incubation
rubrics_metrics.description: avoid authorship. Too early or immoderately employed, it makes the head waste and the heart empty;... he, who sends away through the pen and the press every thought, the moment it occurs to him, will in a short time have sent all away, and will become a mere journeyman of the printing-office, a compositor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not publish every passing thought. Allow ideas to recirculate and mature; reflective reworking preserves vigor and depth in both mind and work. Resist habitually writing solely to produce output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be critical of authoritative reference works; aim for more precise lexicons
rubrics_metrics.description: I should be surprised at hearing from a philosophic and thorough scholar any but very qualified praises of [Johnson's Dictionary]... I refer at present both to omissions and commissions of a more important nature... It is a subject of most serious regret, that the same heavy expenditure... had not been applied to a new Lexicon on a more philosophical plan...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and lexicographers should not accept established authorities uncritically; seek more precise, philosophically-informed vocabularies (including multilingual synonym sets) to capture fine distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match discursive or intuitive mode to subject (discursive vs intuitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus, Philosophy has hitherto been discursive; while Geometry is always and essentially intuitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate mode of presentation: complex philosophical argument often requires discursive treatment; subjects amenable to direct intuition (e.g., geometry) benefit from immediate, intuitive exposition. Respect the epistemic mode of your topic.
